rationale: B wins because "Going's new AI planner lets the airfare pick the destination" is the cleanest story in either batch: a real behavior inversion, not just a product-extension wrapper. A's nearest version, "Going bets the cheap-fare alert is only the top of the trip," is solid but flatter, and its extra "Mistake fares vanish fast" angle needs a customer it does not have. B also asks sharper proof questions, especially whether outbound links earn referral revenue; that could change the whole pitch instead of merely supporting it.
gaps_in_A: "Mistake fares vanish fast" is plausible, but it is not supplied as a fact; without a named member and real booking example, this is a feature description wearing a trench coat.
"If the prevailing push in the space is toward agents that book end-to-end" imports an external market peg, then admits it was not handed one. Correct caution, but the angle is not pitchable yet.
"the alerts-to-planning thesis" is competent trade framing, but it misses the sharper user behavior inversion: the fare picks the destination.
"five shapes exist" overstates readiness. At least one shape is conditional on proof that does not exist in the update.
gaps_in_B: "to convert 2 million free deal-hunters" asserts intent. The update says Premium-only; it does not say Going is using the planner specifically as a conversion play.
"now gates its first AI feature to Premium" invents "first." That word needs proof or it comes out.
"newsletter-born audiences get monetized as software" leans on outside company history not provided in the update. Maybe true, but this judging exercise gave you facts for a reason.
"Most trip-planning tools start from a destination" is a useful frame, but it is a market claim and needs support before it appears in a pitch.
